passage:
In the classroom of the village school, Charu Madam asked for the capital of Assam. “Dispur,” said Rekha. Charu Madam raised one eyebrow. Rekha's stomach dropped. For a second she thought, I am wrong. Then she remembered how Madam's eyebrow goes up when she is curious. “I saw it on the map,” Rekha said quickly. “Guwahati is the biggest city, but Dispur is the capital.”
Charu Madam's mouth curved. “Good. I wondered how you knew the difference.”

qa.q: What did Charu Madam do after Rekha said “Dispur”?
qa.a: She raised one eyebrow.

qa.q: What did Rekha first think the raised eyebrow meant, and how did she change her reading?
qa.a: She first feared it meant she was wrong. Then she recalled that the eyebrow goes up when Madam is curious, so she read it as a question and explained.

qa.q: What worked well in how Rekha responded?
qa.a: She treated the eyebrow as a question and gave her reason, rather than assuming anger or going quiet.

qa.q: How might Charu Madam see the moment?
qa.a: She was probably curious rather than doubtful, and glad to hear the reasoning. The eyebrow was a question, not disapproval.

grounding: A child reads a teacher's raised eyebrow as a question and explains, rather than assuming anger.

passage:
Chen finished explaining his science project on magnets: the paperclip crossing the water in the glass without getting wet. Mr Oskar raised one eyebrow. Chen felt his face go warm. Does he think I cheated? Then he thought, Maybe he wants to know how it works. “I put the magnet outside the glass,” he said, “and moved it slowly along, because the paperclip was inside.”
“Show me,” said Mr Oskar, leaning forward. Chen did it again. Mr Oskar smiled. “Nice, I'd like the class to see that.”

qa.q: What did Chen's project show?
qa.a: It showed the paperclip crossing the water in the glass without getting wet.

qa.q: What did Chen worry about when Mr Oskar raised an eyebrow, and what else did he consider?
qa.a: He worried the teacher thought he cheated, but he also thought Mr Oskar might just want to know how it works, and then answered as though it was a question.

qa.q: What could Chen do if he was not sure what an eyebrow meant?
qa.a: He could ask politely, “Would you like me to explain it again?”, or explain his steps as he did here, which turned doubt into interest.

qa.q: How might Mr Oskar see Chen's reply?
qa.a: As a clear, confident answer to his question, which is why he asked to see it again.

grounding: A child reads a teacher's raised eyebrow as a question and offers an explanation.

passage: Dolma slid her notebook onto the pile, the last one in, with a brown stain across the cover. Kalyani Ma'am picked it up and raised one eyebrow. Dolma's stomach dropped. She's angry. She thinks I'm careless. She wanted to run back to her seat. Instead she remembered her Pala saying a question deserves an answer. “The roof leaked on my table last night,” she said. “I dried it by the stove. The pages are all there.” Kalyani Ma'am's eyebrow came down. She flipped through. “So they are. Thank you for telling me. Next time a plastic cover, maybe?”

qa.q: What was across the cover of Dolma's notebook?
qa.a: A brown stain was across the cover.

qa.q: What was Dolma feeling when Kalyani Ma'am raised one eyebrow?
qa.a: She felt scared and ashamed, thinking the teacher was angry and saw her as careless.

qa.q: Why did explaining work better than running back to her seat?
qa.a: Treating the eyebrow as a question gave Kalyani Ma'am the real reason, the leaking roof, and turned doubt into understanding.

qa.q: What did the raised eyebrow probably mean to Kalyani Ma'am?
qa.a: It likely meant a simple question about the stain, not anger, since she thanked Dolma once she heard the reason.

grounding: Shows a child reading a teacher's raised eyebrow as anger, then treating it as a question and explaining, which works better.

passage: I'm Nazia, and I was next in line for the class presentations. Arnab was showing his poster on the water cycle when Sir raised one eyebrow at the arrow from the clouds back to the sea. Arnab stopped. His voice went sharp. “It's right! I checked!” The class went still. Sir's eyebrow stayed up. “I didn't say it was wrong. I'm asking why it goes that way.” Arnab's ears turned pink. He looked at his poster, then explained that rain falls into the sea too. Sir nodded slowly. “Good. Add a label.” I can't know what Arnab felt, but he sat down very fast.

qa.q: What was Arnab's poster about?
qa.a: Arnab's poster was on the water cycle.

qa.q: Why did Arnab's voice go sharp when Sir raised an eyebrow?
qa.a: He probably felt defensive and embarrassed, reading the eyebrow as a sign Sir thought he was wrong.

qa.q: What could Arnab try next time a teacher raises an eyebrow?
qa.a: He could treat it as a question and simply explain his thinking, as he did in the end, instead of defending himself first.

qa.q: How did Nazia see the moment?
qa.a: Nazia saw the class go still and Arnab sit down fast, but doesn't claim to know what Arnab felt.

grounding: Shows a child reading a teacher's raised eyebrow as disapproval, and how explaining in answer to the question works better.

passage: Monday: Bhupen said the answer to 6 × 7 was 48. Sarita Ma'am raised one eyebrow. Bhupen went red and didn't speak for the rest of the lesson, sure she was cross. Wednesday: At home he told his Dada about it. Dada raised one eyebrow at him, slowly. “What am I saying now?” Bhupen squinted. “Are you asking something?” “I'm asking, ‘Are you sure?’ That's all.” Friday: Bhupen wrote 54 for 6 × 9, and up went Sarita Ma'am's eyebrow. His heart thumped, but he looked again. “I checked. 6 × 9 is 54.” She nodded. “Good. You checked.”

qa.q: What did Bhupen say 6 × 7 was on Monday?
qa.a: Bhupen said the answer to 6 × 7 was 48.

qa.q: What was Bhupen feeling when the eyebrow went up on Friday?
qa.a: He felt nervous, his heart thumping, but more confident than on Monday because he now read the eyebrow as a question.

qa.q: What did Dada teach Bhupen, and how did it help?
qa.a: Dada showed that a raised eyebrow can simply ask “Are you sure?”, so on Friday Bhupen checked and explained instead of going silent.

qa.q: What would Sarita Ma'am have wanted on Monday when she raised her eyebrow?
qa.a: She probably wanted Bhupen to check his answer, not to feel scolded, and his silence may have puzzled her.

grounding: Shows a child learning over several days to read a teacher's raised eyebrow as a question rather than anger.

passage: "Lalremsiami, come and sit. When I, your grandmother Sabina, was about your age, at the school up the hill in Aizawl, our teacher had a famous eyebrow. One day I handed in my sums, smudged and half in pencil. He looked at the page, then at me, and up went one eyebrow. My stomach dropped. I was sure he was furious, and I nearly ran out of the room. But I made myself speak: our lamp had run out of kerosene, so I had finished by the window at dawn. The eyebrow came down. He nodded and said, 'Then next time, tell me first.' That eyebrow was a question, child, not a slap."

qa.q: Why were Sabina's sums smudged and half in pencil?
qa.a: The lamp had run out of kerosene, so Sabina had finished by the window at dawn.

qa.q: What did young Sabina feel when the teacher raised one eyebrow?
qa.a: Sabina felt frightened, with a dropping stomach, and was sure the teacher was furious, though the eyebrow could just as well have meant doubt or a simple question.

qa.q: Which choice in the story turned things around?
qa.a: Sabina chose to explain instead of running out, treating the eyebrow as a question that deserved an answer.

qa.q: How did the teacher likely see the smudged page once Sabina explained?
qa.a: He understood the reason and stopped doubting; his nod and "tell me first" show he was satisfied, not angry.

grounding: It is a grandmother's memory of reading a teacher's raised eyebrow as anger and learning it was a question best answered with an explanation.
